walkthroughs.body_html:
Geographic Perspectives: Global Change — a core area of Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Geographic Perspectives: Global Change brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Geographic Perspectives: Global Change.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How many planetary boundaries did Rockstrom et al identify in 2009?
What happens at a constructive (divergent) plate boundary?
options: At constructive boundaries the plates slide past each other sideways.
At constructive boundaries the plates collide and build mountains.
Plates move apart, magma rises to fill the gap and solidifies, forming new oceanic crust — for example at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
The ITCZ is the boundary between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

mcqs.q: Why is an ageing population a challenge for HICs?
options: Rising dependency ratio means fewer workers support more pensioners through tax, increasing pressure on pensions, healthcare and social care services.
Because old people stop contributing anything to society.
Because old people consume too much food.
At constructive boundaries the plates slide past each other sideways.

mcqs.q: What is the ITCZ and why does it bring rain?
options: The Intertropical Convergence Zone is where trade winds from both hemispheres converge near the equator, forcing air to rise, cool and produce heavy convectional rainfall.
The ITCZ is the boundary between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
Because old people consume too much food.
The ITCZ is a fixed band of permanent storms at the equator.
